JANUS Model — Literature Review

BACOU, Melanie

DRAFT (sources fetched, light verification performed; page-level verification pending)

Apr 30, 2026

An AI-assisted review of JANUS (and JANUS-like) cosmological theories associated with French renowned physicist Jean‑Pierre Petit. The reviews focuses on the family of models that invokes bimetric or multi-metric gravity with positive- and negative-mass sectors as an alternative approach to dark matter and dark energy. This review synthesizes the available preprints (arXiv) and related work by Petit and his collaborators, separates consensus points from disputed claims, and lists concrete open questions and recommended follow-ups.

  • Keywords:
  • janus;
  • petit;
  • bigravity;

This review was produced by an automated pipeline that:

  • Collected candidate sources from arXiv author searches and the Jean‑Pierre Petit Wikipedia page.
  • Downloaded arXiv PDFs and performed per-page text extraction (pdftotext) for verification.
  • Ran a light verifier to find key claims and a full verifier to map claims to specific PDF pages.
  • Extracted figure/table captions and searched for numeric/fit evidence.
  • Performed a reviewer pass to flag unsupported claims and editing issues.

All citations are to arXiv preprints retrieved during the gather step; claims should be cross-checked in the full verifier stage for exact quotations, page numbers, and references to figures and tables.

Primary artifacts are stored under outputs/ (raw PDFs, per-page extracts, caption extracts, verifier and reviewer reports).

Background & Motivation

Jean‑Pierre Petit has authored several papers exploring negative-mass matter and bimetric/bigravity formulations that aim to (a) avoid the runaway instability historically associated with negative masses and (b) provide alternative explanations for galaxy rotation curves and cosmic acceleration without invoking particle dark matter or a cosmological constant. Representative arXiv items retrieved: Petit & d’Agostini ((Petit and D’Agostini 2014), see p.1, p.5), Petit & d’Agostini ((Petit and D’Agostini 2007), see p.10) and ((Petit and D’Agostini 2008), see p.1), and related pieces on negative mass in relativistic quantum mechanics ((Debergh et al. 2018), see p.1).

Visual materials and figures: Petit’s expositions include schematic/topological figures in (Petit and D’Agostini 2008) (e.g., Fig.7–13 on p.11–13) illustrating twin-universe / time-arrow constructions; bigravity/bimetric diagrams and related discussion appear in (Petit and D’Agostini 2007) (see p.10–12); Newtonian/bimetric approximations and the “runaway” discussion are set out in arXiv:1408.2451 (see p.1, p.5–6). Captions and nearby context were extracted to outputs/verifier/captions.md for quick reference.

Core Model Ingredients (summary)

  • Two (or more) metric sectors / “bigravity” structure: the gravitational field is described by two coupled metric tensors (often labelled g+ and g-). Each matter sector minimally couples to its own metric.

  • Positive‑ and negative‑mass matter: a second sector is populated by matter with reversed active gravitational mass (and appropriate sign conventions), producing repulsive inter‑sector gravity while retaining attractive interaction within a same‑sign sector.

  • Coupled field equations: Petit formulates coupled Einstein‑type field equations (one per metric) with coupling terms that govern the inter‑metric interaction; in some versions a Newtonian (bimetric) limit shows modified interaction laws between opposite‑sign masses that can suppress runaway behavior (see arXiv:1408.2451, e.g. Bimetric Newtonian approximation, p.5; also arXiv:0712.0067, p.10).

Note: exact action, coupling constants, and sign conventions vary across Petit’s papers; refer to the primary sources for precise equations (examples: arXiv:0712.0067, arXiv:1408.2451 — see p.10 and p.5 respectively).

Claimed phenomenology / predictions

  • Rotation curves: Petit claims that the gravitational influence of an interpenetrating negative‑mass component (or a halo of negative mass) can reproduce flat galaxy rotation curves without particle dark matter (claimed in Petit’s work). Full per-figure verification did not find numerical rotation‑curve fit tables in the fetched arXiv PDFs; targeted retrieval of Petit’s website/viXra/conference slides is recommended to confirm whether quantitative fits were published outside arXiv.

  • Cosmic acceleration: Petit claims that repulsive inter‑sector interactions can produce large‑scale accelerated expansion without a cosmological constant in some model realizations (see arXiv:0712.0067, e.g. section “About the cosmic acceleration”, p.10; and arXiv:0805.1423, p.22). This is asserted qualitatively in the retrieved preprints; quantitative confrontation with Planck/SDSS-level data is not present in the verified material.

  • Structure formation and lensing: altered clustering and lensing behavior are implied but quantitative structure‑formation predictions and comparisons to CMB/large‑scale structure are not found in the retrieved literature (open; see Open Questions).

Figures, captions, and quantitative evidence (extracted)

I extracted figure/table captions and nearby context from the fetched PDFs to help locate evidentiary material (outputs/verifier/captions.md). Highlights:

  • arXiv:0805.1423 (Petit & d’Agostini) contains didactic/topological figures (Fig.1–Fig.17; see p.10–p.21) illustrating twin‑universe / time‑arrow constructions and related geometrical imagery rather than observational fits.
  • arXiv:0712.0067 includes bimetric/bigravity discussion with schematic figures and supporting text (see p.10–p.12 for bigravity framing).
  • arXiv:1408.2451 contains the Bimetric Newtonian approximation and explicit discussion of the runaway effect (see p.1, p.5–p.6); captions in this paper support theoretical constructs rather than observational fits.
  • arXiv:2206.00300 (not a Petit cosmology paper) contains experimental/numerical figures with explicit captions and fitted curves (FIG.2–FIG.7; see p.10–p.14) — these are hydrodynamics/optics results, illustrative of caption capture but not evidence for JANUS cosmology.
  • arXiv:2208.14562 (instrumentation) contains many fitting/caption examples (best‑fit values, km/s units), showing the verifier can extract numeric fits when present; however those fits are unrelated to JANUS cosmology.

Net result: the caption extraction confirms many schematic and theoretical figures in Petit’s papers, but did not reveal rotation‑curve numerical fits in the arXiv PDFs we fetched. If rotation‑curve fits exist, they likely appear in non‑arXiv venues (author website, slides, or non-indexed reports) — those should be fetched and verified.

Relation to Prior Theoretical Work

  • Negative mass in GR has a long history (Bondi 1957 and follow-ups) and is generally regarded as conceptually possible but troublesome due to runaway solutions when naively combined with positive mass. Petit’s contribution is to propose a coupled/bimetric framework that claims to remove runaway solutions via modified interaction laws in the Newtonian limit (arXiv:1408.2451).

  • Bigravity and multimetric theories have been extensively studied in mainstream GR (e.g., Rosen, massive/bigravity literature); Petit’s work fits into this broad class but often departs in the sign assignments and physical interpretation (see arXiv:0712.0067, 0805.1423 for Petit’s approach).

Reception, verification status, and main criticisms (summary)

  • Publication venues: Many of Petit’s technical presentations and detailed model expositions appear on arXiv (preprints) and the author’s own materials. A substantial portion of the JANUS-related narrative appears outside top-tier peer-reviewed cosmology journals; this affects mainstream visibility and independent verification.

  • Theoretical concerns frequently raised in the literature for negative‑mass ideas include: (a) runaway instabilities in mixed-mass systems unless carefully constrained, (b) potential conflict with energy conditions and standard GR intuitions, and (c) absence of a thorough demonstration that the models reproduce the wealth of cosmological observables (CMB, BAO, lensing, cluster mass profiles) at the precision of Lambda‑CDM. Petit’s bimetric proposals explicitly aim to address (a) but require careful scrutiny of the field equations, constraints, and stability analyses (arXiv:1408.2451).

  • Empirical verification is limited: I found arXiv-level claims and some qualitative fits but not a set of independently reproduced quantitative cosmological fits matching Planck/SDSS/etc. (open; see Open Questions).

Consensus vs. Disagreements

Consensus (provisional)

  • The JANUS family fits within a class of speculative bimetric/negative‑mass proposals studied by a small number of authors. The mathematical idea of coupled metrics and separate matter sectors is well‑formed as a theoretical construct.

  • Historically, naive negative‑mass + positive‑mass mixtures lead to runaway behavior; any claim to have removed runaway solutions must be checked at the full relativistic level and in dynamical N‑body contexts.

Disagreements / contentious claims

  • Whether Petit’s particular coupling choices robustly avoid runaways while preserving accepted tests of GR is disputed in the broader community (few independent verifications found).

  • Claims that JANUS can replace dark matter and dark energy simultaneously are strong; they require matching a broad set of observables. I found no thorough, peer‑reviewed confrontation with CMB + LSS + lensing comparable to Lambda‑CDM (critical gap).

Open questions and recommended follow‑ups

  • Verify field equations: extract and examine the action and field equations from Petit’s primary papers (e.g., arXiv:0712.0067, 1408.2451). Check for well‑posedness, energy conditions, and linear stability.

  • Run N‑body simulations: implement a Newtonian/relativistic toy simulation of two interacting sectors (positive/negative mass) using Petit’s interaction laws to test for runaway suppression and structure formation predictions.

  • Observational discriminants: compute lensing signatures, linear growth rate f(z), and matter power spectrum predictions for JANUS variants and compare to existing surveys (Planck, DES, KiDS).

  • Independent reproduction: search for and encourage independent reproductions of claimed galaxy rotation‑curve fits.

Recommended immediate reading (for a researcher new to JANUS)

  1. Petit & d’Agostini, “Can negative mass be considered in General Relativity ?” (arXiv:1408.2451) — focuses on Newtonian limit and runaway discussion.
  2. Petit, “Bigravity as an interpretation of the cosmic acceleration” (arXiv:0712.0067) — earlier bigravity framing.
  3. Petit & d’Agostini, “Five Dimensional bigravity…” (arXiv:0805.1423) — topological/bigravity variants.
  4. Debergh, Petit, d’Agostini, “On evidence for negative energies…” (arXiv:1809.05046) — negative mass / Dirac equation discussion.

Conclusion (provisional)

JANUS and related negative‑mass/bimetric proposals by Jean‑Pierre Petit present an internally consistent family of theoretical models that aim to address outstanding cosmological puzzles without conventional dark sectors. The hypotheses are speculative and require rigorous checking: the literature retrieved is heavy on arXiv preprints and light on independent, peer‑reviewed reproductions and thorough confrontation with precision cosmology. The next steps are explicit: verify the field equations and stability claims, run dedicated N‑body and lensing calculations, and compare predictions quantitatively to observational datasets.

See outputs/janus-cosmology.provenance.md for the provenance record and list of downloaded sources and verification artifacts.

Time to Migrate this Blog from Distill to Quarto

Mastering Quarto Markdown for literate programming, technical writing, and web publishing

BACOU, Melanie

Oct 1, 2023

A post about literate programming in general and Quarto formats in particular, in which I document migrating this personal blog from Distill to Quarto. Compared to J.J. Allaire’s Distill for R Markdown, Posit® Quarto Markdown uses a new templating system built on top of Bootstrap v5.3.1 with new page and content layouts, extended export formats, and more flexible publishing workflows. This post briefly outlines my process for creating a custom Bootstrap theme for this revamped website, and design tweaks I made along the way.

  • Keywords:
  • theming;
  • bootstrap;
  • ejs;

With the release of Quarto 1.4 (in 2023), markdown-based publishing is gaining popularity, way beyond the scientific community. Multilingual text-based publishing formats (such as Emacs org-mode, Rmarkdown and Jupyter notebooks) that combine executable code chunks with formatted prose greatly simplify the process of drafting, iterating, compiling, documenting, sharing and reproducing computable research experiments.

Old-time researchers1 2 and engineers have long used Emacs Org-Mode (along with its wild hordes of keyboard shortcuts) to achieve similar results thanks to Eric Schulte’s incredible Babel extension (see Schulte et al. 2012) and to John MacFarlane’s Pandoc document converter library – but nowadays Quarto makes use of more efficient script parsers and optimized runtime engines (Sass, Deno, V8) as well as in-browser real-time rendering of documents.

1 For folks born this century, to babel (elips) or to sweave (R) is the process of compiling text documents that include both static markup and compile-time executable scripts.

The concept of Literate programming was introduced in 1984 by the mathematician Donald Knuth and was widely popularized thereafter in the engineering community thanks to org-mode in the Emacs editor.

Emacs Org-Mode was created by the astronomer Carsten Dominik in 2003 and remains to this day one of the most used and madly loved note-taking and GTD (Get-Things-Done) tools, with many of its functionality (agenda, tags, etc.) yet to be ported to any markdown engine.

2 Only keyboard, Baby!

In the process of migrating old articles and code notebooks to the Quarto markdown syntax, I used this article as a template to build a complete Bootstrap theme for the revamped website. This article helped me finetune content placement and notebook execution. Feel free to reuse my mbacou/mb-article Quarto extension and other tidbits.

CSS Grid System

One of Quarto’s many great features is the full flexibility of the Bootstrap v5.3 responsive grid system, with a few handy classes to help precisely position content in a document or on a web page. In particular Quarto now provides:

  • 3 predefined (column-based) page layouts:
    • page-layout: full (home page)
    • page-layout: article (this document), and
    • page-layout: custom to use Boostrap CSS grid system
  • 6 column classes to control content width (shown below)
  • 2 margin classes to shift content into the left or right column (like that XKCD comics):
    • <div class="column-margin">, and
    • <span class="aside">
  • 8 classes to overflow content into the left or right column

For example I use Quarto .column-page CSS class to place a flushed banner directly below the post header section, as a way to highlight static or dynamic content. Here is the R code chunk to achieve this, which generates a <div class="column-page"> element, similar to the map above.

#| column: page
#| eval: false

library(leaflet)
leaflet(width="100%", height="15em") %>% addTiles() %>%
  addMarkers(-8.65406047010657, 41.14426475811268, 
    label="Me, as I'm writing this post. Read on, tips below!", 
    labelOptions=labelOptions(textsize="1rem"))

Grid sizing and spacing are defined in _quarto.yml and may also be modified on a per-document basis, for example by setting:

./_quarto.yml
format:
  html:
    grid:
      body-width: 840px
      sidebar-width: 180px
      margin-width: 240px
      gutter-width: 30px

Color Scheme

Bootstrap works best with a limited set of 8 semantic color names. These are well known to Web designers, and for portability’s sake it is advised to work within this standard and thus avoid complex naming. Optionally Bootstrap provides classes for an additional 10 + 4 colors in both opaque and subtle variants. Most corporate brands stick to a handful of colors, but having a complete categorical palette is useful for more intricate graphical elements and for plots.

Choosing a color scheme is relatively easy – for example start from your favorite photo or graphic and upload it to one of the many on-line color palette generators to extract dominant shades. An alternative is to use a professionally curated R palette, such as one available in the paletteer, RBrewer or viridis packages. See r-charts.com for many such examples.

Below I settled for a 12-color palette that simply matches my decade-old Kubuntu desktop4.

4 KDE, 30 years later, still going strong! My personal KDE color scheme in QGIS and VSCode.

5 Development environment theme creator

Another remarkable tool I have used to generate sensible UI color schemes is themer.dev5 – this masterpiece of a library is designed to generate consistent color schemes across Linux desktops and for many consoles, text editors, and IDEs. Check it out!

Moreover as of Quarto v1.6, the engine now supports externally-defined branding elements (colors, fonts, etc.) provided in standalone _brand.yml files. This is a more unified and flexible approach to organizing document- and project-level branding across multiple output formats6.

6 The good folks at Posit further documented this new feature.

Bringing it altogether: Quarto Format Extension

The final Quarto format was released under its own extension, named mb-article. To use in your own documents, simply install the extension with:

quarto use mbacou/mb-article

And to update the extension thereafter:

quarto update mbacou/mb-article

Publishing Workflow

Finally, the latest Quarto release adds perfectly sensible options to optimize everyone’s publishing workflow, in particular through the use of Draft and Freeze behavior:

  • draft: true

    Tells Quarto that a document may (or may not) be listed / accessible to viewers, and prevents automatic re-tangling.

  • freeze: true

    Tells Quarto to only re-tangle a document on content change, and not every time a site is rebuilt.

  2. Curmi et al. 2013

Visualizing Water: Interactive SVG with D3.js

BACOU, Melanie

2021 Water Accounting (IWMI, FAO)

DRAFT, do not cite

Oct 1, 2021

An exploration of multiple dynamic visualization schemes for hydrological model simulations. This work is part of IWMI WA Dashboard assignment.

  • Keywords:
  • r2d3;
  • ggalluvial;
  • D3.js;

This notebook was first generated in 2021 using R package r2d3 to pass objects between R and the JavaScript DOM. It was re-rendered using Quarto in 2026. Quarto now natively supports D3.js through its integration with Observable JS (OJS), which was created by Mike Bostock, the original author of D3. OJS allows to seamlessly mix D3 visualizations with reactive data exploration.

This notebook is to explore multiple visualization schemes for hydrological model simulations. It’s broken down into 3 parts:

  1. Interactive SVG (this page): add user interactivity to existing SVG sheets (or simplified) designs using low-level D3.js library

  2. Flow diagrams: reshape WA+ model output to create interactive Sankey diagrams with Highcharts.js

  3. Interactive 3D timelapse of river basins: create a 3D map of basin landscape with SVG annotation layers (arrows, etc.)

The D3.js approach is the more flexible but also the more “tedious” to implement. Other approaches will be developed in separate notebooks.

Data Preparation

To validate the different approaches we use sample output datasets provided by IWMI scientists for Mali (Niger river basin) and Kenya (Mara river basin). All hydrological models are written in Python and version controlled to GitHub (e.g. Mali notebooks).

library(rmarkdown)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(stringr)
library(data.table)

if (interactive()) {
  setwd("posts/2021-10-16-svg/")
}

# IMWI color palette
tmp <- fread("./data/IWMI.gpl", skip = 4, header = F)
pal <- grDevices::rgb(tmp[, .(V1, V2, V3)], maxColorValue = 255)
names(pal) <- tmp[, V4]
# Save for reuse
saveRDS(pal, "./data/pal_iwmi.rds")

# Default plot theme
options(ggplot2.discrete.color = pal)
theme_mb <- function(
  base_size = 8,
  base_family = "Roboto Condensed",
  base_fill = pal["light"],
  ...
) {
  theme_minimal(base_size, base_family) +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = base_fill, color = NA),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
      panel.grid = element_line(color = "white"),
      legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
      text = element_text(color = pal["black"], lineheight = .8),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = base_size),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = c("right", "top"),
      legend.key.height = unit(.8, "line")
    ) +
    theme(...)
}
data <- list(
  ken = "/run/media/mbacou/Backup MB/WADashboard/ken/hydroloop_results/csv",
  mli = "/run/media/mbacou/Backup MB/WADashboard/mli/csv_km3"
) |>
  lapply(list.files, pattern = "*.csv", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE) |>
  lapply(data.table) |>
  rbindlist(idcol = "iso3", use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE) |>
  setnames("V1", "path")

data[,
  file := basename(path)
][, `:=`(
  year = str_extract(file, "_[0-9]{4}") %>% str_sub(2, 5) |> as.integer(),
  month = str_extract(file, "[0-9]{4}_[0-9]{1,2}") %>%
    str_sub(6, 7) |>
    as.integer(),
  sheet = str_extract(tolower(file), "sheet[0-9]{1}")
)] |>
  setorder(iso3, year, month, na.last = TRUE)

data[iso3 == "ken", .(iso3, file, sheet, year, month)] |>
  paged_table()

Kenya - List of output files

data[iso3 == "mli", .(iso3, file, sheet, year, month)] |>
  paged_table()

Mali - List of output files

In particular we have yearly model steps for Mali and monthly steps for Kenya that are further aggregated to yearly time spans (by variable), as well as monthly time-series. In Mali only Sheet #1 was produced (Resource Base), but the Kenya analysis includes output variables for all 6 hydro sheets.

Let’s load a sample model output for Kenya for the year 2017.

f <- "sheet1_2017.csv"
ken <- data[iso3 == "ken" & file == f][1, fread(path)]
ken |> paged_table()

sheet1_2017.csv

This file lists 34 output variables grouped into CLASS and SUBCLASS. Units are in km³/year. This categorical data can be represented in a Sankey diagram but not very useful as-is (see next section for more work on this).

library(ggalluvial)

ggplot(
  ken,
  aes(
    axis1 = CLASS,
    axis2 = abbreviate(SUBCLASS),
    axis3 = abbreviate(VARIABLE),
    y = VALUE
  )
) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = CLASS), width = 1 / 4, alpha = .7, color = "white") +
  geom_stratum(width = 1 / 4) +
  geom_text(
    stat = "stratum",
    aes(label = after_stat(stratum)),
    angle = 90,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("class", "subclass", "variable")) +
  labs(y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal)) +
  theme_mb(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

And monthly time-series of Incremental ET by land-use classes:

f <- "sheet1_basin_etincr_monthly.csv"
ken.ts <- data[iso3 == "ken" & file == f][1, fread(path)]
ken.ts |> paged_table()

sheet1_basin_etincr_monthly.csv

We’ll gather all the yearly budgets for now into a long table, and simply visualize the time-series.

f <- data[sheet == "sheet1" & is.na(month) & !is.na(year)]
data <- lapply(1:nrow(f), function(x) {
  fread(f[x, path])[, `:=`(
    iso3 = f[x, iso3],
    sheet = f[x, sheet],
    year = f[x, year]
  )]
}) |>
  rbindlist()

fwrite(data, "./data/data.csv")

ggplot(
  data[VALUE > 0 & SUBCLASS %like% "ET"],
  aes(year, VALUE, color = paste(SUBCLASS, VARIABLE, sep = " "))
) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ toupper(iso3), scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Yearly ET Budgets (kg/m³)", color = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = unname(pal)) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme_mb()

We pass this yearly dataset to the client (web browser) as a JSON array named data. We also pass a default color palette pal (declared above) for convenience.

# Send to OJS runtime
ojs_define(data = data[iso3 == "ken" & year == 2017])
ojs_define(pal = pal)

Interactive Sheets

We work off the existing SVG designs, using D3.js constructs to add data binding and interactions. An important drawback of this approach is that each SVG element (rectangle, arrow, text, etc.) is tied to a data variable, so any change in the underlying data schema (esp. renaming of output variables) would require to manually edit the corresponding SVG template (using a text or vector graphic editor).

There are multiple SVG templates provided in the Kenya code repository (under ./scripts/WAsheets/template/svg). They are shown below.

list.files("./svg", pattern = "*.svg", full.names = TRUE)[
  -c(1:3, 7, 9)
] |>
  knitr::include_graphics()

These sheets incorporate a quantity of domain-specific knowledge, they are used to both teach and communicate about the WA+ modeling approach and simulation results. The PDF documents are produced in the final step of the analysis, typically after the water accounts have been aggregated to a seasonal or yearly time span. The process is somewhat (but not entirely) automated, e.g. the analyst can decide to show or hide elements.

Note that the original templates were created in Inkscape with SVG 1.1 specifications. They are professional printable designs and not optimized for rendering in a browser, so we start by testing whether we can interact and modify these designs using D3. We focus on the Resource Base sheet first.

Inkscape provides multiple templating utilities to “merge” SVG files (with template fields declared in the form %VAR_name% with CSV data in order to batch generate PNG or PDF documents. That system is not limited to merging text labels, colors and sizes can also be read in from an external CSV source1.

1 For example inkscape_merge tool.

Below we load the sheet and proceed to map each box height/width and label to an output variable. We also create a dummy SVG barchart widget to make sure that data is read in and rendered in the browser as we expect.

And we need to import D3.js as an external dependency in this notebook.

Click to render a dummy SVG widget using the sample Kenya data for 2017 (to make sure libraries are loaded).

viewof btn1 = d3.select("#d3ex1")
  .append("button")
  .html("Load Dummy Widget")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary")
  .on("click",  () => fun_barchart());
dd = transpose(data).filter(d => d.VALUE !== 0);

async function fun_barchart(data=dd, el="#d3ex1") {
  
  d3.select(el).selectAll("svg").remove();

  var width = 740;
  var box = 0.6 * width/18;
  var height = box * 21;
  
  const svg = d3.select(el)
    .append("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height])
    .style("width", "100%") 
    .style("height", "auto")
    .append("g")
      .attr("transform", "translate(10, 10)");  
    
  // Add X axis 
  var x = d3.scaleLinear()
    .domain([0, 14])
    .range([0, width]);
  
  svg
    .selectAll("mybar")
    .data(data)
    .enter()
    .append("rect")
    .attr("x", d => x(Math.min(0, d.VALUE)) )
    .attr("y", (_, i) => (i * (box+5)+5) )
    .attr("width", d => 0 )
    .attr("height", box)
    .attr("fill", pal[1])
    .on("mouseover", handleMouseOver)
    .on("mouseout", handleMouseOut);
    
  svg.selectAll("mybar")
      .data(data)
      .enter()
      .append("text")
      .attr("x", d => x(0)+10)
      .attr("y", (_, i) => (i * (box+5) + box)  )
      .style("font-size", box*0.6 + "px")
      .attr("text-anchor", "start")
      .text(d => (d.VALUE.toFixed(2) + " km³/year"));
    
  svg
    .append("g")
    .selectAll("text")
    .data(data)
    .enter()
    .append("text")
    .attr("x", width-20)
    .attr("y", (_, i) => (i * (box+5) + box) )
    .style("font-size", box*.6+"px")
    .attr("text-anchor", "end")
    .text(d => (d.SUBCLASS + " - " + d.VARIABLE));
    
  // Animation
  svg.selectAll("rect")
    .transition()
    .duration(800)
    .attr("width", d => x(Math.abs(d.VALUE)))
    .delay((d,i) => i*100);
};

// Test interactions
function handleMouseOver(d, i) {
   d3.select(this)
   .attr("fill-opacity", .5);
};

function handleMouseOut(d, i) {
  d3.select(this)
  .attr("fill-opacity", 1);
};

D3 is incredibly wordy, but then again it’s flexible! Then we load the original SVG design and progressively add visual effects and data bindings.

async function fun_reset(src="./svg/sheet_1.svg", el="d3ex2", hw=740) {
  var div = d3.select("#" + el);

  var svg = div
    .append("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, hw, hw*0.8])
    .insert("svg:g")
    .attr("class", el); 

  var s = d3.select("." + el);
  s.selectAll("svg").remove();

  // Append external design
  d3.xml(src)
    .then(d => {
    s.node().append(d.documentElement);
    d3.select("." + el)
      .selectAll("rect")
        .on("mouseover", handleMouseOver)
        .on("mouseout", handleMouseOut); 
    });
};

Now that we have the SVG DOM loaded, we can do silly things, like change the text color or highlight some elements. We can also list and return object attributes, which we’ll use later to bind visual elements to their underlying data.

function fun_color(el="d3ex2") {
  d3.select("." + el)
  .select("svg")
  .selectAll("text")
    .style("fill", "white");
    
  d3.select("." + el)
  .select("svg")    
  .selectAll("text[class=data]")
    .style("fill", pal[5])
    .attr("stroke", pal[5])
    .transition()
    .duration(800)
    .attr("transform", "translate(2,2)")
    .transition()
    .duration(800)    
    .attr("transform", "translate(0,0)");
 };
 
function fun_fill(el="d3ex2") {
  d3.select("." + el)
  .selectAll("path")
    .style("fill", pal[0])
    .attr("fill", pal[0]);
 };
 
function fun_group(el="d3ex2", group="") {
  var g = group=="" ? "g" : "g[id=" + group + "]";
    d3.select("." + el)
    .select("svg")
    .selectAll(g)
      .attr("stroke", pal[7])
      .attr("fill-opacity", .4)
      .raise()
      .move(
        Math.floor(Math.random() * 20),
        Math.floor(Math.random() * 10)
        );
};
viewof btn5 = d3.select("#d3ex2")
  .append("button")
  .html("Reset Widget")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-secondary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_reset());

viewof btn2 = d3.select("#d3ex2")
  .append("button")
  .html("Change Text Color")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_color());

viewof btn3 = d3.select("#d3ex2")
  .append("button")
  .html("Change Fill Color")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_fill());

viewof btn4 = d3.select("#d3ex2")
  .append("button")
  .html("Show Groups")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_group());

Optimized SVG

At this point, we need to manually modify (simplify) the original SVG design to clean up paths and to make it easier to select and manipulate (drill through) logical layers and groups of elements. We can create a useful hierarchy in Inkscape and then re-import the modified design here.

Make sure to remove attributes <svg width="" height=""> from the SVG file produced by Inkscape for the design to size properly in its DOM container.

viewof btn9 = d3.select("#d3ex3")
  .append("button")
  .html("Reset Widget")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-secondary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_reset('./svg/sheet_1_edited.svg', 'd3ex3'));

viewof btn6 = d3.select("#d3ex3")
  .append("button")
  .html("Highlight Data")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_color('d3ex3'));

viewof btn7 = d3.select("#d3ex3")
  .append("button")
  .html("Show Inflows")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_group('d3ex3', 'ginflow'));

viewof btn8 = d3.select("#d3ex3")
  .append("button")
  .html("Show Outflows")
  .attr("class", "btn btn-outline-primary me-1")
  .on("click", () => fun_group('d3ex3', 'goutflow'));

Next step is to map text labels and possible cell height to data variables.

HTML Widget

When bound with the yearly model simulation dataset assembled above, the HTML widget now behaves as follows (src: shinyapps.io).

Object model for Sheet #1 is shown in the table below.

model <- fread("./data/sheet_1_schema.csv")
model[, .(id, class, subclass, variable)] |> paged_table()

Rainfall: Merge Ground and Satellite Observations with RFMerge

Recalibrate ERA5 hourly temperatures to CIMIS network ground observations

BACOU, Melanie

Jan 16, 2021

  • Keywords:
  • random forest;
  • ERA5;

While estimating winter season frost risk for almond orchards over Central California, project partners reported significant discrepancies between modeled temperature estimates provided by ERA5-LAND Reanalysis dataset and ground observations. These biases impact the calculation of the daily Frost-Degree-Day index (FDD) used to price insurance coverage.

Here we want to recalibrate ERA5-LAND hourly temperatures to CIMIS ground network observations in order to address ERA5 model biases reported over Central California. The entire procedure involves the following steps:

  • Build CIMIS time-series across OLAM portfolio extent
  • Build DEM covariate (using ERA5-LAND extent and spatial resolution)
  • Use RFMerge procedure1 to produce calibrated hourly raster stacks over the past 10 years (we limit this calibration from Jan-01 to Apr-30 every year)

1 See Baez-Villanueva, O. M., Zambrano-Bigiarini, M., Diego, J., Osorio, G.-, & Mcnamara, I. (2020). Tutorial for merging satellite-based precipitation datasets with ground observations using RFmerge.

This work was initially performed for WorldCover PBC and OLAM US in early 2021. It is somewhat redacted here to omit confidential details.

library(mbutils)
library(lattice)
#library(raster)
library(scales)
library(data.table)
library(zoo)
library(cimir)
library(sf)
library(RFmerge)

if (interactive()) {
  setwd("./posts/2021-01-16-rfmerge/")
}

load("_data/2020-burn_olam_usa_06.RData")

pal <- pal(file = "../../_brand.yml")
my.settings <- list(
  superpose.polygon = list(col = alpha(pal, .6), border = "transparent"),
  strip.background = list(col = pal["light"])
)

Covariate Layers

Define zone of interest (ZOI), load and verify covariate layers.

# Clear workspace, keep only portfolio details
load("./tmp/2020-burn_olam_usa_04.RData")
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("dir", "pts.dt")))

pts <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(
  pts.dt[, .(X, Y)],
  data.frame(pts.dt),
  proj4string = CRS("+init=epsg:4326")
)

usa <- getData("GADM", country = "USA", level = 2)
# Limit ZOI to counties of interest to OLAM
usa <- usa[usa$NAME_2 %in% pts.dt[, unique(adm2_nm)], ]
zoi <- extent(usa)
zoi
# class      : Extent
# xmin       : -121.4844
# xmax       : -117.6166
# ymin       : 34.7902
# ymax       : 38.07786

ERA5-LAND Temperature Validation (California)

Can we justify winter Y2017 corrections to ERA5-LAND temperature grids over central California?

BACOU, Melanie

Dec 3, 2020

This notebook is a sample model bias correction for WorldCover PBC.

  • Keywords:
  • random forest;
  • ERA5;

While estimating winter season frost risk for almond orchards over Central California, project partners reported significant discrepancies between modeled-based temperature estimates provided by ERA5-LAND Reanalysis dataset and ground observations from meteo stations. These biases impact the calculation of daily Frost-Degree-Day index (FDD) used to price insurance coverage.

In this analysis we look into more details at ERA5-LAND temperature estimate biases against ground observations collected from NOAA GHCN network of meteorological stations. In particular:

  • Can we justify Y2017 correction to ERA5-LAND hourly temperature grids over OLAM portfolio?
  • Can we perform a portfolio-wide ERA5-LAND temperature validation against NOAA GHCN ground records?

This work was initially produced for WorldCover PBC and OLAM US in early 2021, and redacted here to omit confidential details.

Income Distribution Cartograms

A side-by-side view of U.S. and Russian income distributions – or when best to use cartograms to convey spatial features

BACOU, Melanie

Dec 2, 2020

In the middle of reading Daniel Huffman’s excellent and highly-recommended blog1, I stumbled on his audacious representation of U.S. median income across states – Stunningly informative! This prompted me to look for comparable statistics for Russia2.

1 Daniel Huffman SomethingAboutMaps

2 WorldMapper gridded population cartograms

Quoting directly from Daniel’s article about the many virtues of equal-area projections:

“Here, an area’s color conveys one dataset, and its size conveys a related dataset that provides some useful context (what portion of the country’s population lives in those various income brackets). Our fallible human brains usually want us to interpret some meaning from variations in the size of areas (which is always a challenge with choropleths), so cartograms leverage that. We usually laud these heavily-distorted choropleths that are most assuredly not equal-area.”
– Daniel Huffman
